The College of Engineering, Physics, and Computing welcomes
transfer applications

from students at any accredited domestic or international institution. In general, courses are evaluated for transfer credit after a student has been accepted. We encourage interested students to contact us directly for more information.

Many transfer and non-traditional students have successfully completed engineering studies after initially completing pre-engineering programs at other institutions. Recognizing that transfer and non-traditional students contribute greatly to our community through diversity, culture, and maturity, Catholic University’s College of Engineering, Physics, and Computing welcomes applications from students from pre-engineering programs.
Admission for Transfer Students

Transfer credit from other accredited colleges and universities is evaluated individually and can be used to satisfy engineering and liberal studies requirements. Engineering transfer courses are evaluated by the College of Engineering, Physics, and Computing. Non-engineering courses (i.e. mathematics, physics, etc.) are evaluated by the relevant school (typically the School of Arts and Sciences but in some case the School of Philosophy or the School of Theology and Religious Studies). Students applying for transfer from certain U.S. or international partner institutions will have their transfer credit approved according to the relevant Transfer Program.

In general, to apply coursework towards the Catholic University degree, the course must 1) be substantially similar to a Catholic University course, 2) be completed with a C- or better grade, and 3) not duplicate previous work.

University policy requires that at least half of the credits required for a Catholic University bachelor’s degree be taken at Catholic University, and that at least 30 of the last 36 credit hours must be taken at Catholic University.
Additional Information for Transfer Students

Catholic University has established formal agreements with several universities and colleges in the U.S. and abroad. These include articulation agreements with regional community colleges, 3+2 agreements with Catholic liberal arts colleges in the United States, and 2+2 agreements with international universities.
Students can begin with pre-engineering study at other institutions then transfer to Catholic University to complete their engineering degree.
The School of Engineering welcomes students from around the world, and has established transfer programs with numerous partner universities.

The Graduate Research Fellowship Program (GRFP) offered by the National Science Foundation (NSF) helps ensure the quality, vitality, and diversity of the scientific and engineering workforce of the United States. The program is open to those who intend to enroll or are enrolled full-time in a research-based Master’s or doctoral degree program in an eligible Field of Study in STEM or STEM education. For more information, please
visit the program website
National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate (NDSEG) Fellowship

The National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate (NDSEG) Fellowship program was established in 1989 by direction of congress as an approach to increasing the number of United States (U.S.) citizens receiving doctoral degrees in science and engineering disciplines of military importance. For more information, please visit the
program website
Paul & Daisy Soros Fellowships for New Americans

The Paul & Daisy Soros Fellowships for New Americans (PD Soros) supports thirty New Americans - immigrants or the children of immigrants - who are pursuing graduate or professional school in the United States. visit the program website
Hertz Fellowship

The Hertz Fellowship is available to college seniors, first-year graduate students, or students in a gap year preparing to apply to graduate school. This fellowship includes a cost-of-education allowance, and a personal stipend valued at up to $250,000.

/programs-admission/scholarships-aid/gra.lead: The College of Engineering, Physics, and Computing and the individual academic departments offer internal scholarships for graduate students who demonstrate academic merit and research potential (in addition to other more specific criteria). Scholarship awardees are selected by the Faculty Scholarship Committee that oversees the selection process in their respective department. These scholarships are competitive and applicants should obtain a faculty recommendation prior to submitting an application.

runs.x: The following list includes both school-level and department-level graduate scholarships. Please make sure to review the selection criteria carefully, prior to asking a faculty member for a recommendation, in order to ensure your eligibility. Once you confirm your eligibility, please fill out the corresponding application form and submit all required documentation (all uploaded materials must be PDF documents). You should also consult with your department chair and/or faculty advisor about how these scholarship awards may impact your other funding sources.
Scholarship applications and materials must be submitted by April 1st
Learn more about these scholarships and to submit your application.

Deans and department chairs nominate the most qualified applicants whose application is complete by Feb. 1 for the University-wide competition for the Knights of Columbus Fellowship and the prestigious Board of Trustees full-tuition scholarship.
The strongest applicants to a doctoral program (high GPA, cumulative verbal and quantitative GRE of at least 312 or equivalent) may be considered for a full-tuition scholarship.
Applicants to Master’s programs with a minimum verbal and quantitative GRE score of 300 are considered for a limited number of half-tuition scholarships.
Students receiving merit funding must be enrolled in their degree program continuously and full-time.
Endowed scholarships are awarded by the department chair, if available. Contact you academic department chair for additional information.

/programs-admission/undergraduate-progra.title: Artificial Intelligence (BS)
/programs-admission/undergraduate-progra.lead: The Bachelor of Science in Artificial Intelligence equips students with the knowledge and skills needed to excel in one of the fastest-growing and most influential fields in technology. The program provides a strong foundation in AI principles, including machine learning, neural networks, and data science, while emphasizing hands-on experience with industry-standard tools and real-world applications. It is among the first undergraduate AI degrees in the country to combine rigorous technical training with a formal ethical framework. Building on the strengths of the University’s Computer Science program, students develop both the technical expertise and the virtue-based perspective needed to create AI solutions that responsibly serve humanity.

blocks.alt: male student at a computer

blocks.x: The Bachelor of Science in Artificial Intelligence provides students with the technical foundation and ethical understanding to shape this rapidly evolving field. Drawing on the Catholic intellectual tradition, our program examines how AI can serve human dignity and the common good while mastering foundational AI concepts, machine learning algorithms, and advanced programming.

items.x: The program provides a strong foundation in machine learning, neural networks, and data science, with hands-on experience using industry-standard tools and real-world applications.
Built for the Workforce, Grounded in Ethics:

Graduates are prepared for careers in AI research, development, and application across various industries, with an added differentiator: training in the ethical frameworks employers increasingly require as AI regulation and governance become boardroom priorities.
Accelerated Path to a Master’s Available:

The college offers an Accelerated Master’s Program that allows motivated undergraduates to begin graduate coursework before completing their bachelor’s degree, compressing the timeline toward an advanced credential.

One of the first undergraduate AI degrees in the country to pair cutting-edge technical training with a deep ethical and humanistic framework, giving graduates a distinctive profile in a crowded job market.

runs.x: At Catholic University, AI education integrates cutting-edge technical training with deep ethical insight. Our program examines how artificial intelligence transforms society, healthcare, and human interaction. Students master not only advanced algorithms and machine learning, but engage with fundamental questions about AI’s role in serving human dignity and the common good. Through research opportunities in our AI labs, internships with industry partners, and specialized tracks in robotics, ethical AI design, and natural language processing, students develop the technical expertise and moral wisdom needed in fields from healthcare to finance. Drawing on Catholic intellectual tradition, we prepare graduates who can both innovate and guide AI development toward advancing human potential.
Graduates of the BS in AI program will:

items.x: Possess strong technical skills in AI and machine learning.
Be prepared for careers in AI research, development, and application across various industries.
Have a deep understanding of the ethical implications and societal impact of AI technologies.

/programs-admission/undergraduate-progra.lead: The Bachelor of Biomedical Engineering at Catholic University blends engineering, biology, and medicine into a powerful, hands‑on undergraduate experience. Students learn to design medical technologies, analyze biological systems, and solve real‑world health challenges through a curriculum that integrates rigorous STEM coursework with labs, design projects, and interdisciplinary collaboration.

blocks.alt: medical lab with a computer screen showing dna

blocks.x: This interdisciplinary field combines aspects of engineering, computer science, biology, chemistry, and medicine to advance human health. Students study biomedical engineering to apply quantitative, analytical, and engineering approaches toward innovative healthcare solutions, including novel medical devices, biological implants, and all the tools of modern medicine and biomedical science.

items.x: A strong liberal studies tradition at Catholic University provides graduates with a broad understanding of engineering as it relates to the global marketplace.
The majority of classes have less than 20 students thereby increasing opportunities for faculty-student interaction!
The Biomedical Engineering (Bachelor of Biomedical Engineering) program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission (EAC) of ABET, and has been for 30+ years.

A set of four undergrad tracks help meet the individual needs and aspirations of students: pre-medical; biomechanics and rehabilitation engineering; bioinstrumentation, medical imaging and telemedicine; and biomaterials and hard tissue engineering.
: Faculty in BE are experts in their respective research areas and bring real-world, contemporary challenges into the classroom.

runs.x: Signature experiences include laboratory‑rich coursework, faculty‑mentored research, and a senior capstone design project where students develop solutions to real biomedical problems. The degree is ABET‑accredited, reflecting national standards of quality and professional preparation.

Graduates leave ready to innovate in medical device development, research labs, healthcare technology, or pursue advanced degrees in engineering, medicine, or related fields, supported by the advantages of studying in Washington, D.C., a hub for hospitals, research institutions, and federal agencies.

Students progress from foundational math and science into specialized biomedical engineering courses, biomechanics, biomaterials, instrumentation, and systems physiology, supported by design‑centered learning and opportunities for undergraduate research. The program offers two pathways: a Regular Track for engineering careers and graduate study, and a Pre‑Med Track for students preparing for medical school.

blocks.x: Chemical Physics majors seek to understand how the universe works. You will take lab coursework ranging from organic chemistry to electricity and magnetism, participate in exciting research, and have the chance to intern at one of D.C.’s many laboratories.

items.x: There is wide demand for graduates who bring the quantitative training that a Physics education provides combined with a deep knowledge of Chemistry.

Students have access to many internships, some of them paid, inside the Department and in labs in the wider research ecosystem that our Department is situated in including JLAB, CERN, NIH, NIST, ARL, NRL, Naval Observatory, and NASA.

runs.x: The Bachelor of Science in Chemical Physics is a program that prepares students for industrial and academic positions that require strong interdisciplinary training in Physics and Chemistry. This is a demanding yet rewarding program that prepares students for further studies at the graduate level or to join the scientific/technical workforce, especially in industries at the cutting edge of engineering and technology.

The selection of courses is designed to give students a strong background in Physics and Chemistry, and includes courses in classical and modern physics (Phys 215, 216, and 406, plus labs 225 and 226), thermodynamics and statistical physics (Phys 425), analytical mechanics (Phys 435), electromagnetic theory (Phys 436), quantum mechanics (Phys 431-432), and mathematical methods of physics (Phys 411-412), as well as the senior seminar in physics (Phys 451-452). In addition, there are eight required courses in chemistry, four required courses in mathematics, and four program electives in mathematics, science, or engineering.
Additional courses in literature, languages, philosophy, religion, the social and behavioral sciences, and the humanities, and 4 free elective courses round out the undergraduate curriculum.

/programs-admission/undergraduate-progra.title: Civil Engineering (BCE)
/programs-admission/undergraduate-progra.lead: The first two years build the analytical foundation every civil engineer works from: three semesters of calculus plus engineering mathematics, university physics, chemistry, engineering mechanics, and solid mechanics, alongside computer programming and computer-aided engineering tools. Design is introduced immediately rather than deferred, students take Introduction to Engineering Design and Profession and the Applied Steel Studio in their first year, and Surveying in the first spring.

blocks.alt: 2 engineers discussing plans

blocks.x: Civil engineers plan, design, build, and maintain the physical systems a society runs on, buildings and bridges, highways and transit, water supply and treatment, and environmental infrastructure. The Bachelor of Civil Engineering is an ABET-accredited, four-year professional degree that pairs a rigorous engineering foundation with a choice of four concentrations, a required professional internship, and a two-semester capstone design project, all in the heart of Washington, D.C.

items.x: 131 credits over four years, on campus in Washington, D.C.
Structural Engineering; Construction Engineering and Management; Transportation Engineering; and Water Resources and Environmental Engineering.
Required for graduation, two for Construction students, and most are paid.
to the 14 knowledge areas of the NCEES Fundamentals of Engineering exam, with an optional FE review course in the senior spring.

runs.x: The junior and senior years move across the full breadth of the discipline. Every student takes theory of structures, fluid mechanics, hydraulics, soil mechanics and the soil laboratory, civil engineering materials, introduction to transportation systems design, introduction to environmental engineering, reinforced concrete design, civil engineering systems, and probability and statistics for engineers. That breadth is deliberate: real civil engineering problems rarely respect sub-discipline boundaries, and graduates are expected to be conversant across all of them both on the licensing exam and in practice.

Six CEE elective courses let students go deep. Four are taken within a chosen concentration, two of which are foundational courses required for that track, and the remaining two may be taken in the same concentration or in another. Completing at least four courses in a track earns an official concentration; electives taken outside the concentration require written advisor approval. The four tracks are Structural Engineering, Construction Engineering and Management, Transportation Engineering, and Water Resources and Environmental Engineering.

A summer internship is a graduation requirement, not a suggestion. Students arrange a position of roughly ten weeks, most are paid, and they may be anywhere in the country or abroad, and then submit a two-page reflective essay countersigned by a company official. Construction Engineering and Management students complete two. The department’s location in the nation’s capital makes this practical: students intern with regional construction companies, engineering consulting firms, and government agencies, and many convert those positions into full-time offers before graduation.

Senior year centers on a two-semester capstone design sequence, supported by a senior seminar and a professional ethics requirement that civil engineering students may satisfy with Ethics and Stewardship in place of Professional Ethics in Engineering. Coursework throughout the degree is mapped to the 14 knowledge areas of the NCEES Fundamentals of Engineering exam, and an optional FE review course is offered in the senior spring. Because the program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission of ABET, graduates are eligible to sit for the FE exam and to pursue registration as Professional Engineers.

Students with a cumulative GPA of 3.2 or higher who have completed 60 credits may apply to the accelerated bachelor’s/master’s program and count two 500-level courses toward both degrees. Students considering this should enroll in the graduate section of eligible CEE electives in consultation with their advisor, a course taken at the 400 level cannot be double-counted after the fact.

About 25 students are admitted to the department each year, so classes are small and students work directly with their professors. Full-time faculty active in funded research teach alongside practicing engineers and government professionals who bring current practice into the classroom, and undergraduates can join faculty research in the department’s laboratories. A departmental advisory council of practicing engineers keeps the curriculum aligned with what employers in the region actually need.

/programs-admission/undergraduate-progra.title: Environmental Engineering (BS)
/programs-admission/undergraduate-progra.lead: Environmental engineering draws on more of the natural sciences than any other engineering discipline, and the curriculum reflects that. Alongside the standard engineering foundation of calculus, engineering mathematics, physics, mechanics, and solid mechanics, students complete general chemistry with laboratory, general chemistry II, analytical chemistry, biology with laboratory, and introduction to earth science. Computer programming and computer-aided engineering tools are taken in the first year, and Introduction to Environmental Engineering arrives in the sophomore spring, early enough to shape the rest of the degree.

runs.x: The junior and senior years build the professional core. Fluid mechanics leads into hydraulics and then into water resources engineering; hydrogeology and contaminant transport covers the subsurface; water and wastewater treatment engineering covers the built water cycle. Air pollution control and introduction to energy and energy systems address the atmospheric and energy sides of the field, and soil mechanics with the accompanying soil laboratory grounds students in the geotechnical behavior that site remediation depends on. Probability and statistics for engineers supports the modeling and monitoring work throughout.

Four environmental electives let students shape a focus, environmental modeling, geographic information systems, applied hydrology, surface water quality, solid waste management, civil engineering systems, or renewable energy and technology. Students choose these in consultation with their advisor, and those planning graduate study often use them to begin the sequence they will continue at the master’s level.

A summer internship is required for graduation. Students arrange a position of roughly ten weeks, most are paid, and they may be anywhere in the country or abroad, and afterward submit a two-page reflective essay countersigned by a company official. In Washington, D.C., environmental engineering students are within reach of federal and regional agencies, water and wastewater utilities, and the environmental consulting firms that serve them.

The degree closes with a two-semester senior capstone design sequence and a senior seminar. Students satisfy the professional ethics requirement through Ethics and Stewardship, a course developed for students working on the built and natural environment. Coursework is mapped to the knowledge areas of the NCEES Fundamentals of Engineering exam, an optional FE review course is offered in the senior spring, and because the program is ABET-accredited, graduates are eligible to sit for the FE and pursue registration as Professional Engineers.

The department’s work in this area is informed by the University’s broader commitment to environmental stewardship, including an initiative on climate change inspired by Pope Francis’s encyclical letter
Laudato Si’
. Students encounter these questions as engineering problems with public consequences, not as abstractions.

Students with a cumulative GPA of 3.2 or higher who have completed 60 credits may apply to the accelerated bachelor’s/master’s program and count two 500-level courses toward both the B.S.Env.E. and a master’s degree. The 500-level section must be the one in which the student enrolls; the substitution cannot be made after the fact.

/programs-admission/undergraduate-progra.lead: The Mechanical Engineering program at The Catholic University of America offers students a distinctive educational experience that combines rigorous technical training with a broad-based liberal education rooted in the Catholic intellectual tradition. Located in the heart of Washington, DC, the program prepares students not only to become skilled engineers but also thoughtful leaders capable of addressing the technical and human challenges of modern society. The curriculum is carefully structured over four years to provide students with a strong academic foundation while also allowing opportunities for personal growth, professional development, and meaningful campus involvement. It is a strong balance between liberal studies and humanities as well as the engineering-specific coursework.

blocks.x: The Mechanical Engineering program at The Catholic University of America combines a rigorous technical education with the broader intellectual and personal development that comes from a strong liberal arts tradition. Students graduate with a solid engineering foundation while also benefiting from opportunities for leadership, athletics, study abroad, and participation in a close-knit university community in the nation’s capital.

items.x: Tailor your coursework to your career goals with our engineering specializations in Aerospace or Energy and the Environment.
Our program meets industry standards for educating the mechanical engineers of tomorrow.
Students have traveled to many international locations including Rome and Ireland.
Upon graduation, students begin careers in a variety of fields including Aeronautical and Space Mission engineering.

runs.x: The foundations for the Mechanical Engineering program are mathematics and the physical sciences, including calculus, differential equations, physics, and chemistry. These subjects form the scientific backbone of engineering and provide students with the analytical tools needed to understand complex mechanical systems. Students develop strong problem-solving abilities and learn how mathematical models and scientific principles are applied to real-world engineering challenges.

All engineering students share a core engineering coursework that stretches across several engineering disciplines. These classes include engineering mechanics, thermodynamics, materials science, electrical circuits, fluid mechanics, engineering design, and computer programming. Students gain hands-on experience in laboratories and design projects that help bridge theory and practice.

Through both the coursework and the opportunities beyond academics-including study abroad programs, Division III athletics, and humanities requirements-the Mechanical Engineering program at Catholic University ultimately seeks to educate the whole person by combining technical excellence, ethical responsibility, intellectual curiosity, and personal development. Graduates leave prepared for successful careers in engineering, advanced study, and leadership roles in a wide variety of fields.

The curriculum emphasizes teamwork, technical communication, and practical problem solving, all of which are essential skills for success in industry and graduate study. In addition to the core engineering coursework, the program offers specialized mechanical engineering topics and technical electives, allowing students to explore areas aligned with their interests and career goals. Students may study vibrations, acoustics, heat transfer, robotics, controls, energy systems, or other advanced subjects.

Senior students complete a capstone design project that integrates the knowledge and skills they have developed throughout the program. These projects often involve collaboration with industry sponsors or research opportunities with faculty members, providing valuable professional experience before graduation.
